claim: The role of striatal pathways in cognitive processing is unclear.
source: The role of striatal pathways in cognitive processing is unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field, presented as background in the abstract.

claim: Interval timing is an elementary cognitive task that requires mice to estimate intervals of several seconds.
source: We studied dorsomedial striatal cognitive processing during interval timing, an elementary cognitive task that requires mice to estimate intervals of several seconds and involves working memory for temporal rules as well as attention to the passage of time.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about the interval timing task used in the study.

claim: Interval timing involves working memory for temporal rules as well as attention to the passage of time.
source: We studied dorsomedial striatal cognitive processing during interval timing, an elementary cognitive task that requires mice to estimate intervals of several seconds and involves working memory for temporal rules as well as attention to the passage of time.
evidence: This statement describes the cognitive components of the interval timing task, supported by citation to Parker et al., 2013 in the Introduction.

claim: D2-MSNs and D1-MSNs exhibited distinct dynamics over temporal intervals as quantified by principal component analyses.
source: We found that D2-MSNs and D1-MSNs exhibited distinct dynamics over temporal intervals as quantified by principal component analyses and trial-by-trial generalized linear models.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 2 and 3, showing PCA results.

claim: D2-MSNs and D1-MSNs exhibited distinct dynamics over temporal intervals as quantified by trial-by-trial generalized linear models.
source: We found that D2-MSNs and D1-MSNs exhibited distinct dynamics over temporal intervals as quantified by principal component analyses and trial-by-trial generalized linear models.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3D, showing GLM slope analysis.

claim: MSN ensemble activity represented the accumulation of temporal evidence in a four-parameter drift-diffusion computational model.
source: MSN recordings helped construct and constrain a four-parameter drift-diffusion computational model in which MSN ensemble activity represented the accumulation of temporal evidence.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling presented in Figure 4 and related text.

claim: The drift-diffusion model predicted that disrupting either D2-MSNs or D1-MSNs would increase interval timing response times.
source: This model predicted that disrupting either D2-MSNs or D1-MSNs would increase interval timing response times and alter MSN firing.
evidence: This is a prediction from the computational model shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: The drift-diffusion model predicted that disrupting either D2-MSNs or D1-MSNs would alter MSN firing.
source: This model predicted that disrupting either D2-MSNs or D1-MSNs would increase interval timing response times and alter MSN firing.
evidence: This is a prediction from the computational model shown in Figure 4.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of D2-MSNs increased interval timing response times.
source: In line with this prediction, we found that optogenetic inhibition or pharmacological disruption of either D2-MSNs or D1-MSNs increased interval timing response times.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of D1-MSNs increased interval timing response times.
source: In line with this prediction, we found that optogenetic inhibition or pharmacological disruption of either D2-MSNs or D1-MSNs increased interval timing response times.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: Pharmacological disruption of D2-MSNs increased interval timing response times.
source: In line with this prediction, we found that optogenetic inhibition or pharmacological disruption of either D2-MSNs or D1-MSNs increased interval timing response times.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E and 5F.

claim: Pharmacological disruption of D1-MSNs increased interval timing response times.
source: In line with this prediction, we found that optogenetic inhibition or pharmacological disruption of either D2-MSNs or D1-MSNs increased interval timing response times.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G and 5H.

claim: Pharmacologically disrupting D2-MSNs changed MSN dynamics.
source: Pharmacologically disrupting D2-MSNs or D1-MSNs also changed MSN dynamics and degraded trial-by-trial temporal decoding.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Pharmacologically disrupting D1-MSNs changed MSN dynamics.
source: Pharmacologically disrupting D2-MSNs or D1-MSNs also changed MSN dynamics and degraded trial-by-trial temporal decoding.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Pharmacologically disrupting D2-MSNs degraded trial-by-trial temporal decoding.
source: Pharmacologically disrupting D2-MSNs or D1-MSNs also changed MSN dynamics and degraded trial-by-trial temporal decoding.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Pharmacologically disrupting D1-MSNs degraded trial-by-trial temporal decoding.
source: Pharmacologically disrupting D2-MSNs or D1-MSNs also changed MSN dynamics and degraded trial-by-trial temporal decoding.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: D2-MSNs and D1-MSNs had opposing dynamics yet played complementary cognitive roles.
source: Together, our findings demonstrate that D2-MSNs and D1-MSNs had opposing dynamics yet played complementary cognitive roles, implying that striatal direct and indirect pathways work together to shape temporal control of action.
evidence: This is a synthesis claim based on the combined results from optogenetic tagging (Figures 2-3), modeling (Figure 4), and disruption experiments (Figures 5-7).

claim: Striatal direct and indirect pathways work together to shape temporal control of action.
source: Together, our findings demonstrate that D2-MSNs and D1-MSNs had opposing dynamics yet played complementary cognitive roles, implying that striatal direct and indirect pathways work together to shape temporal control of action.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings showing that disrupting either pathway produces similar behavioral effects.

claim: The basal ganglia have been heavily studied in motor control.
source: The basal ganglia have been heavily studied in motor control (Albin et al., 1989).
evidence: This is a statement about the historical focus of basal ganglia research, supported by citation.

claim: The basal ganglia are composed of two pathways defined by medium spiny neurons (MSNs) in the striatum: the indirect pathway, defined by D2-dopamine receptor-expressing MSNs (D2-MSNs), and the direct pathway, defined by D1-dopamine receptor-expressing MSNs (D1-MSNs).
source: These subcortical nuclei are composed of two pathways defined by medium spiny neurons (MSNs) in the striatum: the indirect pathway, defined by D2-dopamine receptor-expressing MSNs (D2-MSNs), and the direct pathway, defined by D1-dopamine receptor-expressing MSNs (D1-MSNs).
evidence: This is an established anatomical fact about basal ganglia organization.

claim: It has been proposed that the indirect and direct pathways play opposing roles in movement.
source: It has been proposed that the indirect and direct pathways play opposing roles in movement (Alexander and Crutcher, 1990; Cruz et al., 2022; Kravitz et al., 2010), although recent work identified how these pathways can play more complex and complementary roles (Cui et al., 2013; Tecuapetla et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about prior hypotheses in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Recent work identified how the indirect and direct pathways can play more complex and complementary roles.
source: It has been proposed that the indirect and direct pathways play opposing roles in movement (Alexander and Crutcher, 1990; Cruz et al., 2022; Kravitz et al., 2010), although recent work identified how these pathways can play more complex and complementary roles (Cui et al., 2013; Tecuapetla et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about recent findings in the field, supported by citations.

claim: MSNs receive dense input from both motor and cognitive cortical areas.
source: MSNs receive dense input from both motor and cognitive cortical areas (Averbeck et al., 2014; Graybiel, 1997; Middleton and Strick, 2000), but the respective roles of D2-MSNs and D1-MSNs in cognitive processing are largely unknown.
evidence: This is an anatomical fact about MSN connectivity, supported by citations.

claim: The respective roles of D2-MSNs and D1-MSNs in cognitive processing are largely unknown.
source: MSNs receive dense input from both motor and cognitive cortical areas (Averbeck et al., 2014; Graybiel, 1997; Middleton and Strick, 2000), but the respective roles of D2-MSNs and D1-MSNs in cognitive processing are largely unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in current knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: Understanding basal ganglia cognitive processing is critical for diseases affecting the striatum such as Huntington's disease, Parkinson's disease, and schizophrenia.
source: Understanding basal ganglia cognitive processing is critical for diseases affecting the striatum such as Huntington's disease, Parkinson's disease, and schizophrenia (Andreasen, 1999; Hinton et al., 2007; Narayanan and Albin, 2022).
evidence: This is a statement about the clinical relevance of the research, supported by citations.

claim: Pharmacological and brain stimulation therapies directly modulate D2-MSNs, D1-MSNs, and downstream basal ganglia structures such as the globus pallidus or subthalamic nucleus.
source: Furthermore, pharmacological and brain stimulation therapies directly modulate D2-MSNs, D1-MSNs, and downstream basal ganglia structures such as the globus pallidus or subthalamic nucleus.
evidence: This is a statement about current therapeutic approaches, based on established clinical knowledge.

claim: Interval timing requires cognitive resources including working memory for temporal rules and attention to the passage of time.
source: Interval timing provides an ideal platform to study cognition in the striatum because timing (1) requires cognitive resources including working memory for temporal rules and attention to the passage of time Parker et al., 2013
evidence: This is a statement about the cognitive demands of interval timing, supported by citation.

claim: Interval timing is reliably impaired in human striatal diseases such as Huntington's disease, Parkinson's disease, and schizophrenia.
source: (2) is reliably impaired in human striatal diseases such as Huntington's disease, Parkinson's disease, and schizophrenia Merchant and de Lafuente, 2014
evidence: This is a statement about clinical observations in human diseases, supported by citation.

claim: Interval timing requires nigrostriatal dopamine that modulates MSNs.
source: (3) requires nigrostriatal dopamine that modulates MSNs Emmons et al., 2017; Gouvêa et al., 2015; Matell et al., 2003; Mello et al., 2015; Monteiro et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2018
evidence: This is a statement about the neurochemical basis of interval timing, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Interval timing can be rigorously studied in animal models.
source: (4) can be rigorously studied in animal models (Balci et al., 2008; Buhusi and Meck, 2005; Kim et al., 2017; Parker et al., 2017; Parker et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about the feasibility of studying interval timing in animals, supported by citations.

claim: Striatal MSNs encode time across multiple intervals by time-dependent ramping activity or monotonic changes in firing rate across a temporal interval.
source: We and others have found that striatal MSNs encode time across multiple intervals by time-dependent ramping activity or monotonic changes in firing rate across a temporal interval (Emmons et al., 2017; Gouvêa et al., 2015; Mello et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about prior findings on MSN activity patterns, supported by citations.

claim: Disrupting either D2-dopamine receptors (D2) or D1-dopamine receptors (D1) powerfully impairs interval timing by increasing estimates of elapsed time.
source: Past work has shown that disrupting either D2-dopamine receptors (D2) or D1-dopamine receptors (D1) powerfully impairs interval timing by increasing estimates of elapsed time (Drew et al., 2007; Meck, 2006).
evidence: This is a statement about prior pharmacological findings, supported by citations.

claim: Similar behavioral effects were found with systemic or local infusion of D2 or D1 antagonists locally within the dorsomedial striatum.
source: Similar behavioral effects were found with systemic (Stutt et al., 2024) or local infusion of D2 or D1 antagonists locally within the dorsomedial striatum (De Corte et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about prior experimental findings, supported by citations.

claim: In 30 mice, switch response times were 9.3 s (8.4–9.7; median (IQR)).
source: In 30 mice, switch response times were 9.3 s (8.4–9.7; median (IQR))
evidence: This is a quantitative behavioral measurement from the study.

claim: Four D2-Cre mice had a switch response time of 8.2 (7.7–8.7) s.
source: We studied dorsomedial striatal D2-MSNs and D1-MSNs using a combination of optogenetics and neuronal ensemble recordings in nine transgenic mice (four D2-Cre mice switch response time 8.2 (7.7–8.7) s
evidence: This is a quantitative behavioral measurement from the study.

claim: Five D1-Cre mice had a switch response time of 9.7 (7.0–10.3) s.
source: five D1-Cre mice switch response time 9.7 (7.0–10.3) s; rank sum p = 0.73
evidence: This is a quantitative behavioral measurement from the study.

claim: There was no significant difference in switch response times between D2-Cre and D1-Cre mice (rank sum p = 0.73).
source: five D1-Cre mice switch response time 9.7 (7.0–10.3) s; rank sum p = 0.73
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of behavioral data.

claim: 32 putative D2-MSNs were tagged in the study.
source: We tagged 32 putative D2-MSNs and 41 putative D1-MSNs in a single recording session during interval timing.
evidence: This is a count of neurons recorded in the study.

claim: 41 putative D1-MSNs were tagged in the study.
source: We tagged 32 putative D2-MSNs and 41 putative D1-MSNs in a single recording session during interval timing.
evidence: This is a count of neurons recorded in the study.

claim: There were no consistent differences in overall firing rate between D2-MSNs and D1-MSNs.
source: There were no consistent differences in overall firing rate between D2-MSNs and D1-MSNs (D2-MSNs: 3.4 (1.4–7.2) Hz; D1-MSNs 5.2 (3.1–8.6) Hz; F = 2.7, p = 0.11
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of neuronal firing rates.

claim: D2-MSNs had an average firing rate of 3.4 (1.4–7.2) Hz.
source: There were no consistent differences in overall firing rate between D2-MSNs and D1-MSNs (D2-MSNs: 3.4 (1.4–7.2) Hz
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of neuronal activity.

claim: D1-MSNs had an average firing rate of 5.2 (3.1–8.6) Hz.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of neuronal activity.

claim: For 32 putative D2-MSNs average PETH activity increased over the 6-s interval immediately after trial start.
source: For 32 putative D2-MSNs average PETH activity increased over the 6-s interval immediately after trial start, whereas for 41 putative D1-MSNs, average PETH activity decreased.
evidence: This is a description of neuronal activity patterns observed in the data, shown in Figure 2G.

claim: For 41 putative D1-MSNs, average PETH activity decreased over the 6-s interval immediately after trial start.
source: For 32 putative D2-MSNs average PETH activity increased over the 6-s interval immediately after trial start, whereas for 41 putative D1-MSNs, average PETH activity decreased.
evidence: This is a description of neuronal activity patterns observed in the data, shown in Figure 2H.

claim: D2-MSNs and D1-MSNs had differences in activity early in the interval (0–5 s; F = 4.5, p = 0.04 accounting for variance between mice).
source: Accordingly, D2-MSNs and D1-MSNs had differences in activity early in the interval (0–5 s; F = 4.5, p = 0.04 accounting for variance between mice) but not late in the interval (5–6 s; F = 1.9, p = 0.17 accounting for variance between mice).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of neuronal activity patterns.

claim: D2-MSNs and D1-MSNs did not have differences in activity late in the interval (5–6 s; F = 1.9, p = 0.17 accounting for variance between mice).
source: Accordingly, D2-MSNs and D1-MSNs had differences in activity early in the interval (0–5 s; F = 4.5, p = 0.04 accounting for variance between mice) but not late in the interval (5–6 s; F = 1.9, p = 0.17 accounting for variance between mice).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of neuronal activity patterns.

claim: PC1 exhibited time-dependent ramping and explained 54% of variance among tagged MSNs.
source: PCA identified time-dependent ramping activity as PC1 (Figure 3A), a key temporal signal that explained 54% of variance among tagged MSNs (Figure 3B; variance for PC1 p = 0.009 vs 46 (44–49)% for any pattern of PC1 variance derived from random data; Narayanan, 2016).
evidence: This is a result from principal component analysis shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: D2-MSNs had negative PC1 scores (PC1 for D2-MSNs: –3.4 (−4.6 to 2.5)).
source: Consistent with population averages from Figure 2G, H, D2-MSNs and D1-MSNs had opposite patterns of activity with negative PC1 scores for D2-MSNs and positive PC1 scores for D1-MSNs (Figure 3C; PC1 for D2-MSNs: –3.4 (−4.6 to 2.5)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from PCA shown in Figure 3C.

claim: D1-MSNs had positive PC1 scores (PC1 for D1-MSNs: 2.8 (−2.8 to 4.9)).
source: PC1 for D1-MSNs: 2.8 (−2.8 to 4.9); F = 8.8, p = 0.004 accounting for variance between mice
evidence: This is a quantitative result from PCA shown in Figure 3C.

claim: PC1 scores were significantly different between D2-MSNs and D1-MSNs (F = 8.8, p = 0.004 accounting for variance between mice).
source: PC1 for D1-MSNs: 2.8 (−2.8 to 4.9); F = 8.8, p = 0.004 accounting for variance between mice; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Cohen's d = 0.7; power = 0.80
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of PC1 scores between neuron types.

claim: PC1 scores for D2-MSNs were significantly less than 0 (signrank D2-MSN PC1 scores vs 0: p = 0.02).
source: Importantly, PC1 scores for D2-MSNs were significantly less than 0 (signrank D2-MSN PC1 scores vs 0: p = 0.02), implying that because PC1 ramps down, D2-MSNs tended to ramp up.
evidence: This is a statistical test comparing PC1 scores to zero.

claim: PC1 scores for D1-MSNs were significantly greater than 0 (signrank D1-MSN PC1 scores vs 0: p = 0.05).
source: Conversely, PC1 scores for D1-MSNs were significantly greater than 0 (signrank D1-MSN PC1 scores vs 0: p = 0.05), implying that D1-MSNs tended to ramp down.
evidence: This is a statistical test comparing PC1 scores to zero.

claim: D2-MSNs had significantly different slopes (–0.01 spikes/s (−0.10 to 0.10)) from D1-MSNs (–0.20 (−0.47 to −0.06)) in trial-by-trial GLM analysis (F = 8.9, p = 0.004 accounting for variance between mice).
source: GLM analysis also demonstrated that D2-MSNs had significantly different slopes (–0.01 spikes/s (−0.10 to 0.10)), which were distinct from D1-MSNs (–0.20 (−0.47 to −0.06; Figure 3D; F = 8.9, p = 0.004 accounting for variance between mice
evidence: This is a result from generalized linear modeling shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Trial-by-trial GLM slope was strongly correlated with PC1 scores (PC1 scores vs GLM slope r = –0.60, p = 10–8), explaining 37% of variance.
source: Trial-by-trial GLM slope was strongly correlated with PC1 scores in Figure 3A–C (PC1 scores vs GLM slope r = –0.60, p = 10–8), explaining 37% of variance.
evidence: This is a correlation analysis between two measures of neuronal activity.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of D2-MSNs increased switch response times (Laser Off: 8.6 s (8.3–9.3); Laser On: 10.2 s (9.4–10.2); signed rank p = 0.002, Cohen's d = 1.7).
source: We found that D2-MSN inhibition reliably increased switch response times (Figure 5A, B; Laser Off: 8.6 s (8.3–9.3); Laser On: 10.2 s (9.4–10.2); signed rank p = 0.002, Cohen's d = 1.7).
evidence: This is an experimental result from optogenetic manipulation shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Control experiments in D2-cre mice without opsins using identical laser parameters found no reliable effects.
source: To control for heating and nonspecific effects of optogenetics, we performed control experiments in D2-cre mice without opsins using identical laser parameters; we found no reliable effects for opsin-negative controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a control experiment result shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: DDM predictions were highly concordant with D2-MSN inhibition behavioral data (R2 Data vs Model = 0.95).
source: Remarkably, DDM predictions were highly concordant with D2-MSN inhibition behavioral data (R2 Data vs Model = 0.95; Figure 4—figure supplement 3) as well as with behavioral data from laser off trials (R2 Data vs Model = 0.94; parameters chosen to fit laser off trials; Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between model predictions and experimental data.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of D1-MSNs increased switch response times (Laser Off: 8.7 (8.0–9.1) s; Laser On: 10.5 (9.6–11.1) s; signed rank p = 0.03, Cohen's d = 1.4).
source: In six D1-Cre mice (three female), optogenetic inhibition of dorsomedial striatal D1-MSNs increased switch response times (Figure 5C, D; Laser Off: 8.7 (8.0–9.1) s; Laser On: 10.5 (9.6–11.1) s; signed rank p = 0.03, Cohen's d = 1.4).
evidence: This is an experimental result from optogenetic manipulation shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: Control experiments in D1-cre mice without opsins found no reliable effects.
source: As with D2-MSNs, we found no reliable effects with opsin-negative controls in D1-MSNs (figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is a control experiment result.

claim: DDM predictions were highly concordant with D1-MSN inhibition behavioral data (R2 Data vs Model = 0.95).
source: DDM predictions again were highly concordant with D1-MSN inhibition behavioral data R2 Data vs Model = 0.95; parameters chosen to fit D1-MSN inhibition trials andwith laser off trials (R2 Data vs Model = 0.94; Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between model predictions and experimental data.

claim: Systemic D2 blockade with sulpiride (12.5 mg/kg IP) increased switch response times relative to saline sessions (saline: 8.9 (8.4–9.8) s; D2 blockade: 10.1 (9.4–10.8) s; signed rank p = 0.002, Cohen's d = 1.0).
source: We used sulpiride (12.5 mg/kg intraperitoneally (IP)) to block D2-dopamine receptors in 10 wild-type mice, which increased switch response times relative to saline sessions (median (IQR); saline: 8.9 (8.4–9.8) s; D2 blockade: 10.1 (9.4–10.8) s; signed rank p = 0.002, Cohen's d = 1.0; Figure 5E, F).
evidence: This is an experimental result from pharmacological manipulation shown in Figure 5E and 5F.

claim: There was no difference in switch response time between saline sessions and laser-off trials from D2-MSN optogenetic inhibition in D2-Cre mice (rank sum p = 0.31).
source: There was no difference in switch response time between saline sessions and laser-off trials from D2-MSN optogenetic inhibition in D2-Cre mice, implying that in optogenetic sessions, D2-MSN inhibition did not disrupt behavior during laser-off trials (rank sum p = 0.31).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison between experimental conditions.

claim: Systemic D1 blockade with SCH23390 (0.05 mg/kg IP) increased switch response times (saline: 9.7 s (9.0–9.9); D1 blockade: 10.1 s (9.3–11.4); signed rank p = 0.04, Cohen d = 0.7).
source: In the same 10 wild-type mice, systemic drugs blocking D1-dopamine receptors (D1 blockade; SCH23390 0.05 mg/kg IP) increased switch response times (saline: 9.7 s (9.0–9.9); D1 blockade: 10.1 s (9.3–11.4); signed rank p = 0.04, Cohen d = 0.7; Figure 5G, H)
evidence: This is an experimental result from pharmacological manipulation shown in Figure 5G and 5H.

claim: There was no difference between saline sessions and D1-MSN inhibition laser-off trials in D1-Cre mice (rank sum p = 0.18).
source: Once again, there was no difference between saline sessions and D1-MSN inhibition laser-off trials in D1-Cre mice (rank sum p = 0.18).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison between experimental conditions.

claim: Inhibiting D2-MSNs in the dorsomedial striatum did not change nosepoke duration.
source: We found no evidence that inhibiting D2-MSNs in the dorsomedial striatum changed task-specific movements such as nosepoke duration (i.e., time of nosepoke entry to exit; Figure 5—figure supplement 3) or switch traversal time between the first and second nosepokes (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a negative result from movement analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Inhibiting D2-MSNs in the dorsomedial striatum did not change switch traversal time between the first and second nosepokes.
source: We found no evidence that inhibiting D2-MSNs in the dorsomedial striatum changed task-specific movements such as nosepoke duration (i.e., time of nosepoke entry to exit; Figure 5—figure supplement 3) or switch traversal time between the first and second nosepokes (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a negative result from movement analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: D1-MSN inhibition did not change nosepoke duration.
source: Similarly, we found no evidence that D1-MSN inhibition changed nosepoke duration (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) or traversal time (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a negative result from movement analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: D1-MSN inhibition did not change traversal time.
source: Similarly, we found no evidence that D1-MSN inhibition changed nosepoke duration (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) or traversal time (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a negative result from movement analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Disrupting D2-MSNs or D1-MSNs did not change switch response time standard deviations.
source: Furthermore, disrupting D2-MSNs or D1-MSNs did not change switch response time standard deviations or the number of rewards (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a negative result shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Disrupting D2-MSNs or D1-MSNs did not change the number of rewards.
source: Furthermore, disrupting D2-MSNs or D1-MSNs did not change switch response time standard deviations or the number of rewards (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a negative result shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: 99 MSNs were analyzed in sessions with saline, D2 blockade, and D1 blockade.
source: We analyzed 99 MSNs in sessions with saline, D2 blockade, and D1 blockade.
evidence: This is a count of neurons analyzed in the pharmacology recording experiments.

claim: MSNs were matched across sessions based on waveform and interspike intervals with high similarity (correlation coefficient between matched MSN waveforms: saline vs D2 blockade r = 1.00 (0.99–1.00)).
source: We matched MSNs across sessions based on waveform and interspike intervals; waveforms were highly similar across sessions (correlation coefficient between matched MSN waveforms: saline vs D2 blockade r = 1.00 (0.99–1.00 rank sum vs correlations in unmatched waveforms p = 3 × 10–44
evidence: This is a validation of the neuron matching procedure.

claim: There were no consistent changes in MSN average firing rate with D2 blockade (saline: 5.2 (3.3–8.6) Hz; D2 blockade 5.1 (2.7–8.0) Hz; F = 1.1, p = 0.30 accounting for variance between MSNs).
source: There were no consistent changes in MSN average firing rate with D2 blockade or D1 blockade (saline: 5.2 (3.3–8.6) Hz); D2 blockade 5.1 (2.7–8.0) Hz; F = 1.1, p = 0.30 accounting for variance between MSNs
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of firing rates across conditions.

claim: There were no consistent changes in MSN average firing rate with D1 blockade (D1 blockade 4.9 (2.4–7.8) Hz; F = 2.2, p = 0.14 accounting for variance between MSNs).
source: D1 blockade 4.9 (2.4–7.8) Hz; F = 2.2, p = 0.14 accounting for variance between MSNs; Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of firing rates across conditions.

claim: PC1 explained 54% of neuronal variance in the pharmacology recording experiments.
source: The first component (PC1), which explained 54% of neuronal variance, exhibited 'time-dependent ramping', or monotonic changes over the 6-s interval immediately after trial start (Figure 6F, G; variance for PC1 p = 0.001 vs 46 (45–47)% for any pattern of PC1 variance in random data; Narayanan, 2016).
evidence: This is a result from PCA shown in Figure 6F and 6G.

claim: PC1 scores shifted with D2 blockade (PC1 scores for D2 blockade: –0.6 (−3.8 to 4.7) vs saline: –2.3 (−4.2 to 3.2), F = 5.1, p = 0.03 accounting for variance between MSNs).
source: Interestingly, PC1 scores shifted with D2 blockade (Figure 6H; PC1 scores for D2 blockade: –0.6 (−3.8 to 4.7) vs saline: –2.3 (−4.2 to 3.2), F = 5.1, p = 0.03 accounting for variance between MSNs
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of PC1 scores shown in Figure 6H.

claim: PC1 scores shifted with D1 blockade (PC1 scores for D1 blockade: –0.0 (−3.9 to 4.5), F = 5.8, p = 0.02 accounting for variance between MSNs).
source: PC1 scores also shifted with D1 blockade (Figure 6H; PC1 scores for D1 blockade: –0.0 (−3.9 to 4.5), F = 5.8, p = 0.02 accounting for variance between MSNs
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of PC1 scores shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Saline sessions generated strong temporal predictions for the first 6 s of the interval immediately after trial start (0–6 s; R2 = 0.91 (0.83–0.94)).
source: Saline sessions generated strong temporal predictions for the first 6 s of the interval immediately after trial start (0–6 s; R2 = 0.91 (0.83–0.94)) with weaker predictions for later epochs (6–12 s: R2 = 0.55 (0.34–0.70); rank sum p = 0. 000002 vs 0–6 s, Cohen d = 2.0; 12–18 s: R2 = 0.18 (0.10–0.62); rank sum p = 0.000003 vs 0–6 s, Cohen d = 2.4
evidence: This is a result from temporal decoding analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Temporal decoding early in the interval (0–6 s) was degraded with D2 blockade (R2 = 0.69 (0.58–0.84); rank sum p = 0.0002 vs saline, Cohen d = 1.4).
source: We found that temporal decoding early in the interval (0–6 s) was degraded with either D2 blockade (R2 = 0.69 (0.58–0.84); rank sum p = 0.0002 vs saline, Cohen d = 1.4) or D1 blockade (R2 = 0.71 (0.47–0.87); rank sum p = 0.004 vs saline, Cohen d = 1.1; Figure 7D)
evidence: This is a result from temporal decoding analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Temporal decoding early in the interval (0–6 s) was degraded with D1 blockade (R2 = 0.71 (0.47–0.87); rank sum p = 0.004 vs saline, Cohen d = 1.1).
source: We found that temporal decoding early in the interval (0–6 s) was degraded with either D2 blockade (R2 = 0.69 (0.58–0.84); rank sum p = 0.0002 vs saline, Cohen d = 1.4) or D1 blockade (R2 = 0.71 (0.47–0.87); rank sum p = 0.004 vs saline, Cohen d = 1.1; Figure 7D)
evidence: This is a result from temporal decoding analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Later in the interval (6–12 and 12–18 s), there were no significant differences between saline sessions and D2 or D1 blockade.
source: Later in the interval (6–12 and 12–18 s), there were no significant differences between saline sessions and D2 or D1 blockade (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a negative result from temporal decoding analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Mice were trained to perform an interval timing task in which they had to respond by switching nosepokes after a 6-s interval.
source: We trained mice to perform an interval timing task in which they had to respond by switching nosepokes after a 6-s interval (in gray shade in all panels).
evidence: This is a description of the behavioral task shown in Figure 1A.

claim: On 50% of trials, mice were rewarded for a nosepoke after 6 s at the designated 'first' front nosepoke.
source: On 50% of trials, mice were rewarded for a nosepoke after 6 s at the designated 'first' front nosepoke; these trials were not analyzed.
evidence: This is a description of the task structure.

claim: On 50% of trials, mice were rewarded for switching to the 'second' nosepoke; initial nosepokes at the second nosepoke after 18 s triggered reward when preceded by a first nosepoke.
source: On the remaining 50% of trials, mice were rewarded for switching to the 'second' nosepoke; initial nosepokes at the second nosepoke after 18 s triggered reward when preceded by a first nosepoke.
evidence: This is a description of the task structure.

claim: Switch response time was defined as the moment mice depart the first nosepoke prior to second nosepoke arrival.
source: Switch response time was defined as the moment mice depart the first nosepoke prior to second nosepoke arrival.
evidence: This is a definition of the key behavioral measure.

claim: Switch responses are a time-based decision guided explicitly by temporal control of action.
source: Because cues are identical and on for the full trial on all trials, switch responses are a time-based decision guided explicitly by temporal control of action.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral task design.

claim: Mice switch nosepokes only if they do not receive a reward at the first nosepokes after the 6-s interval.
source: Indeed, mice switch nosepokes only if they do not receive a reward at the first nosepokes after the 6-s interval.
evidence: This is a description of the behavioral contingency in the task.

claim: Responses at the first nosepoke peaked at 6 s.
source: Responses at the first nosepoke peaked at 6 s, and switch responses peaked after 6 s.
evidence: This is a description of behavioral data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Switch responses peaked after 6 s.
source: Responses at the first nosepoke peaked at 6 s, and switch responses peaked after 6 s.
evidence: This is a description of behavioral data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Nosepoking at the second nosepoke was only rewarded after 18 s, so second nosepokes tended to be highly skewed.
source: Because nosepoking at the second nosepoke was only rewarded after 18 s, second nosepokes tended to be highly skewed.
evidence: This is a description of behavioral data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: DeepLabCut tracking revealed increased velocity after trial start and then constant velocity throughout the trial.
source: DeepLabCut tracking of position during interval timing from a single mouse behavioral session revealed increased velocity after trial start and then constant velocity throughout the trial.
evidence: This is a description of movement tracking data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: D2-MSNs in the indirect pathway project from the striatum to the globus pallidus external segment (GPe) and internal segment (GPi).
source: D2-MSNs in the indirect pathway, which project from the striatum to the globus pallidus external segment (GPe; sagittal section) and internal segment (GPi)
evidence: This is an anatomical description shown in Figure 2A.

claim: D1-MSNs project from the striatum to the GPe, GPi, and substantia nigra (SNr).
source: D1-MSNs, which project from the striatum to the GPe, GPi, and substantia nigra (SNr; sagittal section).
evidence: This is an anatomical description shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Neurons that fired within 5 ms of light stimulation were considered optically tagged putative D2-MSNs or D1-MSNs.
source: We identified D2-MSNs or D1-MSNs by their response to brief pulses of 473 nm light; neurons that fired within 5 ms were considered optically tagged putative D2-MSNs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is a description of the optogenetic tagging criteria.

claim: Work by our group and others has uniformly identified PC1 as a linear component among corticostriatal neuronal ensembles during interval timing.
source: Work by our group and others has uniformly identified PC1 as a linear component among corticostriatal neuronal ensembles during interval timing (Bruce et al., 2021; Emmons et al., 2020; Emmons et al., 2019; Emmons et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2017; Narayanan et al., 2013; Narayanan and Laubach, 2009; Parker et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about prior findings, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Two-parameter gamma distributions strongly accounted for the model dynamics (D2-MSNs: Gamma parameters α = 6.08, β = 0.69, R2 Gamma vs Model = 0.99).
source: Interestingly, we observed that two-parameter gamma distributions strongly accounted for the model dynamics (D2-MSNs: Gamma parameters α = 6.08, β = 0.69, R2 Gamma vs Model = 0.99; D1-MSNs α = 5.89, β = 0.69; R2 Gamma vs Model = 0.99; Figure 4C, D, dotted black lines; Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a result from model fitting shown in Figure 4C, D and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Gamma distributions provided a surprisingly good approximation for the probability distribution and cumulative distribution functions of mouse switch response times (R2 Data vs Gamma = 0.94 for D1-MSNs and for D2-MSNs).
source: Gamma distributions also provided a surprisingly good approximation for the probability distribution and cumulative distribution functions of mouse switch response times (Figure 1B–D; R2 Data vs Gamma = 0.94 for D1-MSNs and for D2-MSNs).
evidence: This is a result from model fitting to behavioral data.

claim: All procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) at the University of Iowa (Protocol #0062039).
source: All procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) at the University of Iowa, and all experimental methods were performed in accordance with applicable guidelines and regulations (Protocol #0062039).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: Recent work by the authors shows that D2 and D1 blockades have similar effects in both sexes.
source: Our recent work shows that D2 and D1 blockades have similar effects in both sexes (Stutt et al., 2024).
evidence: This is a statement about prior findings from the authors' group, supported by citation.

claim: Mice were 85% food restricted and motivated with 20 mg sucrose pellets.
source: Mice were 85% food restricted and motivated with 20 mg sucrose pellets (Bio-Serv, Flemington, NJ).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Cues were identical on all trial types and lasted the entire duration of the trial (6 or 18 s).
source: Cues were identical on all trial types and lasted the entire duration of the trial (6 or 18 s).
evidence: This is a description of the task design.

claim: Traversal time was defined as the duration between first nosepoke exit and second nosepoke entry and is distinct from switch response time when animals departed the first nosepoke.
source: Traversal time was defined as the duration between first nosepoke exit and second nosepoke entry and is distinct from switch response time when animals departed the first nosepoke.
evidence: This is a definition of a behavioral measure.

claim: Nosepoke duration was defined as the time between first nosepoke entry and exit for the switch response times only.
source: Nosepoke duration was defined as the time between first nosepoke entry and exit for the switch response times only.
evidence: This is a definition of a behavioral measure.

claim: Trials were self-initiated, but there was an intertrial interval with a geometric mean of 30 s between trials.
source: Trials were self-initiated, but there was an intertrial interval with a geometric mean of 30 s between trials.
evidence: This is a description of the task timing.

claim: Optogenetic viruses were injected into the dorsal striatum (0.5 µl of virus, +0.9, ML +/–1.3, DV –2.7).
source: Craniotomies were drilled above bilateral dorsal striatal anatomical targets, and optogenetic viruses (AAV5-DIO-eNHPR2.0 (halorhodopsin), AAV5-DIO-ChR2(H134R)-mcherry (ChR2), or AAV5-DIO-cherry (control) from the University of North Carolina Viral Vector Core) were injected into the dorsal striatum (0.5 µl of virus, +0.9, ML +/–1.3, DV –2.7).
evidence: This is a description of the surgical procedure.

claim: Fiber optics were positioned in the dorsal striatum (AP +0.9, ML +/–1.3, DV –2.5).
source: Either fiber optics (Doric Lenses, Montreal Quebec; AP +0.9, ML +/–1.3, DV –2.5) or 4 × 4 electrode or optrode arrays (AP +0.4, ML –1.4, DV –2.7 on the left side only; Microprobes, Gaithersburg, MD) were positioned in the dorsal striatum.
evidence: This is a description of the surgical procedure.

claim: Optical inhibition was delivered via bilateral patch cables for the entire trial duration of 18 s via 589 nm laser light at 12 mW power on 50% of randomly assigned trials.
source: In animals injected with optogenetic viruses, optical inhibition was delivered via bilateral patch cables for the entire trial duration of 18 s via 589 nm laser light at 12 mW power on 50% of randomly assigned trials.
evidence: This is a description of the optogenetic manipulation procedure.

claim: Units with mean post-stimulation spike latencies of ≤5 ms and a stimulated-to-unstimulated waveform correlation ratio of >0.9 were classified as putative D2-MSNs or D1-MSNs.
source: Units with mean post-stimulation spike latencies of ≤5 ms and a stimulated-to-unstimulated waveform correlation ratio of >0.9 were classified as putative D2-MSNs or D1-MSNs (Ryan et al., 2018; Shin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a description of the neuron classification criteria, supported by citations.

claim: The sulpiride dosage was 12.5 mg/kg, 0.01 ml/g.
source: The sulpiride dosage was 12.5 mg/kg, 0.01 ml/g, and the SCH23390 was administered at a dosage of 0.05 mg/kg, 0.01 ml/g.
evidence: This is a description of the drug dosages used.

claim: SCH23390 was administered at a dosage of 0.05 mg/kg, 0.01 ml/g.
source: The sulpiride dosage was 12.5 mg/kg, 0.01 ml/g, and the SCH23390 was administered at a dosage of 0.05 mg/kg, 0.01 ml/g.
evidence: This is a description of the drug dosages used.

claim: Single units were defined as those (1) having a consistent waveform shape, (2) being a separable cluster in PCA space, and (3) having a consistent refractory period of at least 2 ms in interspike interval histograms.
source: Single units were defined as those (1) having a consistent waveform shape, (2) being a separable cluster in PCA space, and (3) having a consistent refractory period of at least 2 ms in interspike interval histograms.
evidence: This is a description of the spike sorting criteria.

claim: Spike activity was analyzed for all cells that fired between 0.5 and 20 Hz over the entire behavioral session.
source: Spike activity was analyzed for all cells that fired between 0.5 and 20 Hz over the entire behavioral session.
evidence: This is a description of the inclusion criteria for neuronal analysis.

claim: Putative MSNs were separated from striatal fast-spiking interneurons based on hierarchical clustering of the waveform peak-to-trough ratio and the half-peak width.
source: Putative MSNs were further separated from striatal fast-spiking interneurons based on hierarchical clustering of the waveform peak-to-trough ratio and the half-peak width (fitgmdist and cluster.m; Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Berke, 2011).
evidence: This is a description of the neuron classification method, supported by citation.

claim: Kernel density estimates of firing rates were calculated across the interval (–4 s before trial start to 22 s after trial start) binned at 0.2 s, with a bandwidth of 1.
source: We calculated kernel density estimates of firing rates across the interval (–4 s before trial start to 22 s after trial start) binned at 0.2 s, with a bandwidth of 1.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis method.

claim: All data and statistical approaches were reviewed by the Biostatistics, Epidemiology, and Research Design Core (BERD) at the Institute for Clinical and Translational Sciences (ICTS) at the University of Iowa.
source: All data and statistical approaches were reviewed by the Biostatistics, Epidemiology, and Research Design Core (BERD) at the Institute for Clinical and Translational Sciences (ICTS) at the University of Iowa.
evidence: This is a statement about the statistical review process.

claim: All code and data are made available at https://narayanan.lab.uiowa.edu/article/datasets.
source: All code and data are made available at https://narayanan.lab.uiowa.edu/article/datasets.
evidence: This is a statement about data availability.

claim: For all neuronal analyses, variability between animals was accounted for using generalized linear mixed-effects models and incorporating a random effect for each mouse into the model.
source: For all neuronal analyses, variability between animals was accounted for using generalized linear mixed-effects models and incorporating a random effect for each mouse into the model, which allows us to account for inherent between-mouse variability.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical analysis approach.

claim: p-values <0.05 were interpreted as significant.
source: p-values <0.05 were interpreted as significant.
evidence: This is a statement about the statistical significance threshold.
